opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The way I see it, a few frontier labs are building incredibly capable general models, and that's great. But a general model is trained against a general notion of what "good" looks like. Every company has its own idea of what good looks like for its product, its users, and its workflows, and a lot of that is tacit. It's in their codebase, their support tickets, the judgment calls their best employees make every day. You can get some of the way there with prompting and context engineering. But at some point, if you want a model that really internalizes your definition of success, you want to optimize against it directly.

That's why I'm excited about reinforcement learning in particular. With pretraining or even supervised fine-tuning, the bottleneck has always been data. You need huge amounts of it, and it has to look like the outputs you want. RL changes the question. Now it's less "do you have a million examples?" and more "can you write down what success means?" Can you build an environment, a set of tasks, and a reward signal, whether that's unit tests passing, a rubric, a judge model, or some business metric? Companies have far more of that kind of knowledge than they have clean training data. So RL makes training accessible to many more organizations.

I also think there's a strategic piece. If your entire product is a prompt on top of someone else's API, your moat is pretty thin, and you're exposed to whatever changes happen upstream. If you own the environments, the evals, and the reward functions that encode your domain expertise, that's a durable asset. Even if you swap the base model every six months, you can retrain on top of it. The environment is the thing that compounds.

The honest caveat is that it's still hard today. The tooling is immature, the infrastructure is expensive and finicky, and many teams don't yet have the instinct for how to design a good environment or avoid reward hacking. That's a big part of why I care about open-source tooling and shared environments. My view is that it shouldn't take a team of fifty research engineers to do a good RL run on a model you own. If we can make that feel more like normal software engineering, you can write an environment, test it, and train against it. Then I think you'll see a long tail of companies building specialized models that beat general ones on the things they actually care about. That's a healthier ecosystem than one where everyone just rents intelligence from a handful of providers.

r001.rationale: It says specialized models can outperform general ones on company priorities, but does not state that long experience at a company can outweigh exceptional general intelligence.

r002.rationale: It says prompting and context engineering only go part of the way toward capturing tacit company knowledge, but does not clearly state that training-developed expertise is almost impossible to replicate in a short prompt.

r003.rationale: It calls company environments, evals, and reward functions durable assets and says the environment compounds even when the base model changes.

r004.rationale: It says AI training could feel more like normal software engineering and become accessible to more organizations, but does not draw the stated parallel between falling barriers to software development and AI research.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the way to frame it is that right now, the most interesting work in AI is happening at a tiny number of labs, and most of what the rest of the world gets is the artifact that comes out the other end. You get a model, you get an API, and you adapt your product around whatever that model happens to be good at. That's fine for a lot of use cases, but it means the frontier is defined by what a handful of teams decide to prioritize, and your company's problem is almost never one of those priorities.

What changes when you can train yourself is that you stop being a consumer of someone else's roadmap. If you have a specific environment, a specific set of tasks, a specific notion of what "good" looks like for your users, you can actually push the model toward that. And especially with RL, that's where the leverage is now. The pretraining phase is mostly about broad capability, and you probably don't want to redo that. But the post-training phase, the part where you teach the model to actually do your job well, that's where a company's own data and its own reward signal are the thing nobody else has. That's a real moat, and it only becomes a moat if you have the ability to turn it into weights.

There's also a knowledge argument that I think gets underrated. Training is how you learn what these models can and can't do. If you only ever prompt, you develop intuitions, but they're surface-level. When you've actually run a training loop and watched a reward curve go up, or more often watched it go sideways and had to figure out why, you understand the system in a totally different way. I'd rather have ten thousand teams building that understanding than ten.

And honestly, I think a lot of the "you shouldn't train your own models" advice was correct two years ago and is getting less correct every month. The tooling is better, the open models are much better starting points, and the cost of a meaningful post-training run has come way down. The question isn't really whether it's possible anymore. It's whether people have the recipes and infrastructure to do it without needing a research lab's worth of expertise. That's the gap I care about closing.

r001.rationale: The response says a company’s specific tasks and priorities can guide training, but it does not compare long company experience with exceptional general intelligence.

r002.rationale: It says training gives a deeper understanding than prompting, but does not state that this expertise is almost impossible to reproduce with a short prompt.

r003.rationale: It describes company data and reward signals as a potential moat, but does not present institutional knowledge as compounding over time.

r004.rationale: It says AI training tools and costs have improved, but does not draw a parallel with falling barriers to software development.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest value is that companies know things about their work that are hard to capture in a general-purpose model. They know what a good outcome looks like, where the tricky cases are, and which mistakes are expensive. Enabling them to train a model gives them a way to turn that knowledge into better behavior.

That doesn’t mean every company needs to pretrain a model from scratch. For a lot of companies, the useful thing is taking a capable model and adapting it to a particular task, with feedback from the people who actually do that work.

And I think the key is making that feedback loop accessible. Can you measure whether the model is doing a good job? Can you identify where it fails, train on that, and see an improvement? If you can make that process reliable, companies can start improving AI for their own needs instead of waiting for the next general model release.

r001.rationale: The response says companies hold useful work-specific knowledge, but does not compare long experience at a company with exceptional general intelligence when that expertise is the bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss prompts or say that training-developed expertise is hard to reproduce in a short prompt.

r003.rationale: It describes using feedback to train and improve a model, but does not clearly present institutional knowledge as compounding over time.

r004.rationale: It does not draw a parallel between lower barriers to software development and lower barriers to AI research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is giving companies a way to turn what they know into a system that actually works for them. A general-purpose model can do a lot, but it doesn’t automatically know what great work looks like inside your business, or which mistakes really matter.

Training lets you take that expertise—the examples, the feedback, the judgment of your best people—and use it to improve the model. Then you can get a feedback loop where using the system helps you discover where it falls short, and those failures become opportunities to make it better.

I don’t think every company needs to train a foundation model from scratch. The interesting question is whether a company can take an existing model and reliably teach it something valuable about its own work. If that becomes accessible, a lot more people get to decide what AI is good at.

r001.rationale: The response says a model needs to learn what great work looks like inside a business, but it does not compare company experience with exceptional general intelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes training on examples, feedback, and judgment, but does not say this expertise is nearly impossible to replicate with a short prompt.

r003.rationale: It describes using feedback and failures to improve a model, but does not state that institutional knowledge compounds over time.

r004.rationale: It discusses making AI training accessible but draws no parallel to software development barriers falling alongside AI research barriers.
